scenarios.title: The three SOCs
scenarios.situation: A company has separate SOC teams for the US, EU, and APAC, each needing isolated incidents but shared threat intel.
scenarios.prompt: What workspace design fits?
choices: One workspace per region (data residency + isolated queues) with cross-workspace hunting and shared watchlists/TI
One workspace for everything worldwide
A workspace per analyst
No workspaces; use email
scenarios.why: Workspace design balances data residency, RBAC isolation, and cost: regional workspaces keep EU data in the EU and queues separate, while cross-workspace queries, Lighthouse delegation, and shared threat intel preserve unified defense.
scenarios.hint: Isolation per region but shared hunting — how many workspaces?

scenarios.title: The firewall logs
scenarios.situation: A Palo Alto firewall's logs need to reach Sentinel in near real time for correlation.
scenarios.prompt: Which ingestion path fits?
choices: The Palo Alto data connector (CEF via Syslog/AMA) — normalized into CommonSecurityLog
Manual CSV uploads
Emailing logs to the SOC
A custom VM running scripts
scenarios.why: Sentinel's data connectors (including CEF/Syslog via the Azure Monitor Agent) stream third-party logs into normalized tables like CommonSecurityLog. Connector choice determines parsing, latency, and which analytics rules can fire.
scenarios.hint: Which table do CEF firewall logs land in, and what ships them?

scenarios.title: The legacy agent
scenarios.situation: The SOC still uses the legacy Log Analytics agent (MMA/OMS) on servers, which Microsoft is retiring.
scenarios.prompt: What is the migration path?
choices: Azure Monitor Agent with data collection rules (DCRs) — granular, per-source collection replacing MMA
Keeping MMA forever
No agent at all
A third-party agent
scenarios.why: AMA + DCRs replace the legacy MMA: data collection rules define exactly what to collect from which machines (Syslog facilities, Windows events, CEF), reducing noise and cost versus the old agent's broad collection.
scenarios.hint: What replaces the retiring MMA, and what controls what it collects?

scenarios.title: The 2-year mandate
scenarios.situation: Compliance requires security logs retained 2 years, but interactive hunting only needs 90 days hot.
scenarios.prompt: What retention design fits?
choices: Interactive retention 90 days + archive (long-term) tier for the remainder — cheap cold storage, searchable via restore/search jobs
2 years of interactive retention
Deleting after 90 days
Exporting to USB drives
scenarios.why: Log Analytics splits retention: interactive (hot, fast KQL) plus archive tier (cheap, 12-year capable) with search/restore jobs for investigations. Paying interactive rates for 2-year-old logs is the expensive mistake.
scenarios.hint: Hot for hunting, cold for compliance — which two retention settings?

scenarios.title: The noisy connector
scenarios.situation: One verbose connector ingests 500 GB/day of low-value logs, dominating the Sentinel bill.
scenarios.prompt: What reduces cost without losing security value?
choices: Filter at collection (DCRs), drop noisy facilities, or route low-value logs to the auxiliary/basic tier — ingest less, not blind
Deleting the connector
Paying without question
Sampling alerts only
scenarios.why: Sentinel cost control happens at ingestion: DCR filtering, dropping chatty Syslog facilities, and using basic/auxiliary log tiers for high-volume low-value data. You can't analyze what you never ingest — so filter noise, not signal.
scenarios.hint: Where is the cheapest place to reduce log volume?

scenarios.title: The MSSP model
scenarios.situation: An MSSP must manage Sentinel across 40 customer tenants without 40 separate logins.
scenarios.prompt: What enables multi-tenant SOC operations?
choices: Azure Lighthouse — delegated resource management across tenants from one SOC workspace view
Sharing customer admin passwords
40 browser profiles
Emailing incidents around
scenarios.why: Lighthouse delegates subscription/resource-group management to the MSSP's tenant — one pane of glass, customer tenants retain ownership and can revoke. It's the designed multi-tenant operations model.
scenarios.hint: How does one SOC operate 40 tenants without shared passwords?

scenarios.title: Sentinel Workspaces: Design Decision
scenarios.situation: You need to make an architecture/design decision for Sentinel Workspaces in a Sc 200 environment. Multiple approaches are viable, but each has tradeoffs.
scenarios.prompt: Which approach best balances the competing concerns for this Sentinel Workspaces scenario?
choices: Analyze the requirements, evaluate each option against constraints (performance, cost, complexity, maintainability), select the approach with the best tradeoff profile, and document the decision rationale including rejected alternatives.
Choose the most familiar approach — comfort matters more than fit.
Choose the newest technology — latest is always best.
Delay the decision — more analysis is always better.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Architecture decisions require structured evaluation: (1) Clarify requirements and constraints, (2) Enumerate viable options, (3) Score each against weighted criteria, (4) Select the best tradeoff, (5) Document why others were rejected. This prevents both analysis paralysis and reckless choices in Sentinel Workspaces design.
scenarios.hint: Think about how senior engineers make decisions — it's not gut feel, it's structured evaluation.
evidence: Review Sentinel Workspaces requirements and constraints.

scenarios.title: Sentinel Workspaces: Expert Scenario
scenarios.situation: An advanced Sentinel Workspaces challenge in a Sc 200 environment requires expert-level judgment. The situation involves multiple interacting factors.
scenarios.prompt: What is the expert-level approach to this Sentinel Workspaces challenge?
choices: Systematically analyze all factors, prioritize by impact and urgency, implement the solution with verification at each step, and document the approach for the team.
Apply the most common solution immediately without analysis.
Defer to someone else — this is too complex.
Try random approaches until something works.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Expert Sentinel Workspaces work in Sc 200 requires: systematic analysis (understand all factors), prioritization (impact × urgency), verified implementation (check each step), and documentation (team learning). This disciplined approach distinguishes senior practitioners.
scenarios.hint: What separates expert practice from guessing?

scenarios.title: The failed logons
scenarios.situation: An analyst needs: failed Windows logons (EventID 4625) in the last 24h, grouped by target account, top 20.
scenarios.prompt: Which KQL query does this?
choices: SecurityEvent | where EventID == 4625 | where TimeGenerated > ago(24h) | summarize count() by TargetUserName | top 20 by count_ desc
SELECT * FROM SecurityEvent WHERE EventID=4625
SecurityEvent | take 20
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{ID=4625}
scenarios.why: KQL pipelines filter (where), aggregate (summarize ... by), and rank (top). SecurityEvent carries Windows events; 4625 is the failed-logon ID. SQL syntax doesn't run in Log Analytics.
scenarios.hint: Filter, group-count, rank — which pipeline?

scenarios.title: The user-to-IP link
scenarios.situation: The analyst has suspicious IPs from the firewall and needs the usernames behind them from sign-in logs.
scenarios.prompt: Which KQL technique connects the two tables?
choices: join — e.g., suspicious IPs joined to SigninLogs on IPAddress to pull UserPrincipalName
Two separate queries eyeballed manually
A union of unrelated tables
Exporting to Excel
scenarios.why: join correlates tables on a shared key (IPAddress here) — the core hunting move linking network evidence to identity evidence. Choose inner/leftouter deliberately; watch for many-to-many fan-out.
scenarios.hint: Two tables, one shared key — which operator links them?

scenarios.title: The beaconing suspicion
scenarios.situation: An analyst suspects malware beaconing — regular outbound connections every 60 seconds to a rare domain.
scenarios.prompt: What visualization exposes the pattern?
evidence: CommonSecurityLog | where DestinationHostName == 'evil.example' | summarize c=count() by bin(TimeGenerated, 1m) | render timechart
choices: render timechart of connection counts binned per minute — beaconing shows as unnaturally regular spikes
A pie chart of total bytes
A table of raw logs
An alert with no context
scenarios.why: Timecharts reveal periodicity: human traffic is bursty and irregular; beaconing is metronomic. summarize count() by bin(TimeGenerated, 1m) | render timechart turns a hunch into visible evidence.
scenarios.hint: Which visualization makes 'every 60 seconds' obvious?

scenarios.title: The impossible travel
scenarios.situation: A user logs in from New York and Tokyo 20 minutes apart.
scenarios.prompt: What detects this, and what is the caveat?
choices: Identity Protection's impossible-travel detection / anomaly analytics rules — but VPNs and mobile carriers cause false positives needing tuning
A firewall rule
Password expiry
Ignoring it
scenarios.why: Anomaly-based analytics (ML rules, Identity Protection) flag deviations like impossible travel; but VPN egress locations and carrier NAT create false positives. Hunting means tuning thresholds and validating before escalating.
scenarios.hint: What detects the anomaly, and what commonly fakes it?

scenarios.title: The hypothesis hunt
scenarios.situation: Threat intel reports a new ransomware group using a specific LOLBIN pattern. No alerts have fired.
scenarios.prompt: What should the hunter do?
choices: Proactive hypothesis-driven hunting — write KQL for the TTP across tables before alerts exist, then create an analytics rule if found
Wait for alerts
Reimage random machines
Disable the intel feed
scenarios.why: Hunting is proactive: start from intel/TTPs, query broadly for the behavior, and convert validated hunts into scheduled analytics rules. Waiting for alerts means waiting to be a victim.
scenarios.hint: No alerts yet — what proactive motion finds the TTP first?

scenarios.title: The VIP list
scenarios.situation: Hunters repeatedly look up whether IPs belong to the company's partner ranges or known-bad lists.
scenarios.prompt: What makes this lookup reusable?
choices: Watchlists — uploaded reference data joinable in KQL (e.g., partner CIDRs, VIP users, terminated employees)
Hardcoding IPs in every query
A spreadsheet on someone's desktop
Memory
scenarios.why: Watchlists store reference data (IP ranges, VIPs, service accounts) as queryable tables joined into hunts and analytics rules — turning tribal knowledge into reusable detection logic.
scenarios.hint: Where does reference data live so every hunt can join it?

scenarios.title: KQL Hunting: Production Incident
scenarios.situation: A production KQL Hunting system is experiencing degraded performance. Users are affected. You need to diagnose and resolve quickly without making things worse.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct incident response sequence for this KQL Hunting degradation?
choices: Assess impact and declare incident severity, check recent changes (deployments, config changes), review key metrics to isolate the layer, implement the least-risky mitigation first, verify recovery, then conduct a blameless post-mortem.
Immediately restart all KQL Hunting components — fastest way to resolve.
Roll back the last deployment without investigation — it's always the deployment.
Wait and monitor — it might resolve itself.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Incident response follows: (1) Assess impact (how bad? who's affected?), (2) Check recent changes (what changed?), (3) Isolate via metrics (which layer?), (4) Mitigate with least risk (don't make it worse), (5) Verify recovery, (6) Post-mortem (prevent recurrence). Skipping steps in KQL Hunting incidents causes extended outages.
scenarios.hint: Remember the incident response phases from the lessons. What's the order?
evidence: Review KQL Hunting requirements and constraints.

scenarios.title: The alert storm
scenarios.situation: One compromised host generates 200 related alerts; analysts triage each one separately and drown.
scenarios.prompt: What groups them into one investigation?
choices: Incident grouping — analytics rules correlate related alerts into a single incident by entity and time
More analysts
Deleting alerts
A bigger workspace
scenarios.why: Sentinel groups alerts sharing entities (host, user, IP) within a time window into one incident — the unit of investigation. Alert-per-row triage is the anti-pattern; incidents are the workflow.
scenarios.hint: What turns 200 related alerts into one investigation?

scenarios.title: The 2 AM page
scenarios.situation: An analyst gets a 'massive login failures' incident at 2 AM with no context.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct triage sequence?
choices: Scope (which entities, blast radius) → validate (true/false positive) → contain → eradicate → recover → lessons learned
Delete the incident
Reimage everything immediately
Wait until morning
scenarios.why: Triage follows the incident lifecycle: understand scope first (entities graph, timeline), validate it's real, then contain before eradicating. Reimaging before scoping destroys evidence and may miss persistence.
scenarios.hint: Before touching anything, what two questions must triage answer?

scenarios.title: The known-good noise
scenarios.situation: A vulnerability scanner triggers 'port scan' incidents nightly — always benign, always auto-closed by analysts.
scenarios.prompt: What automates this handling?
choices: An automation rule — auto-close with a comment when the source is the known scanner IP
Deleting the analytics rule
Ignoring all port-scan incidents
A playbook that reimages the scanner
scenarios.why: Automation rules handle incident lifecycle chores (assign, change status/severity, close) on trigger conditions — the first automation layer. Playbooks (Logic Apps) do the heavy enrichment/response; rules do the triage routing.
scenarios.hint: Which automation layer auto-closes known-benign incidents?

scenarios.title: The enrichment gap
scenarios.situation: Every phishing incident needs: URL detonation, sender history, and user notification — done manually in 30 minutes.
scenarios.prompt: What automates the response workflow?
choices: A playbook (Logic Apps) triggered on incident creation — enriches, acts, and notifies automatically
An automation rule alone — can't call APIs or branch logic
A KQL query
A meeting
scenarios.why: Playbooks are Logic Apps wired to Sentinel triggers: they query TI, detonate URLs, isolate hosts via Defender, open tickets, and notify — SOAR orchestration. Automation rules trigger them and handle simple status changes.
scenarios.hint: Which SOAR construct runs multi-step API-driven response?

scenarios.title: The playbook permission
scenarios.situation: A playbook needs to isolate machines via Defender for Endpoint — but with least privilege.
scenarios.prompt: How should the playbook authenticate?
choices: Its own managed identity granted only the Defender 'isolate machine' permission — scoped, auditable, no stored secrets
The SOC lead's personal account
A shared admin password in the workflow
No authentication
scenarios.why: Playbooks are privileged automation — they deserve their own managed identity with minimal API permissions. A playbook running as a human inherits that human's breadth; a scoped identity limits what automation can do if abused.
scenarios.hint: What identity should powerful automation run as?

scenarios.title: The aging incident
scenarios.situation: High-severity incidents sit unassigned for days; nobody notices until the weekly review.
scenarios.prompt: What operational control prevents this?
choices: Incident SLAs/aging alerts + assignment automation rules — unassigned or aging incidents escalate automatically
More dashboards nobody watches
A weekly meeting
Hope
scenarios.why: SOC operations need aging/escalation mechanics: automation rules assign on creation, and SLA-style alerts fire when high-severity incidents age unassigned. Process enforced by automation beats process documented in a wiki.
scenarios.hint: What ensures no high-severity incident sits unassigned?

scenarios.title: Incidents & Playbooks: Code Review Finding
scenarios.situation: During code review, you notice a Incidents & Playbooks implementation that works but has potential issues. The author is a junior developer who is eager to merge.
scenarios.prompt: How do you handle this Incidents & Playbooks code review as a senior team member?
choices: Provide specific, actionable feedback: explain the issue, why it matters, suggest a concrete fix, and offer to pair on the solution. Approve the approach but request changes on the implementation.
Approve immediately — it works, and you don't want to discourage the junior.
Reject outright with 'this is wrong' — they'll figure it out.
Rewrite the code yourself — faster than explaining.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Effective code review for Incidents & Playbooks: (1) Be specific about the issue (not 'this is bad'), (2) Explain the impact (why it matters), (3) Suggest a fix (don't just criticize), (4) Offer help (mentorship). This builds both better Incidents & Playbooks code and better engineers.
scenarios.hint: Think about the goal of code review — it's not just gatekeeping, it's team growth.
evidence: Review Incidents & Playbooks requirements and constraints.

scenarios.title: The five portals
scenarios.situation: Analysts pivot between separate portals for endpoint, identity, email, and cloud-app alerts on one attack.
scenarios.prompt: What unifies the investigation?
choices: The Microsoft Defender portal (XDR) — unified incidents correlating Defender for Endpoint/Identity/Office 365/Cloud Apps signals
Five browser tabs
A spreadsheet
Sentinel alone — it ingests but doesn't replace XDR correlation
scenarios.why: Defender XDR natively correlates signals across its workloads into single cross-domain incidents with one entity graph. Sentinel then extends this with third-party/SIEM breadth — XDR depth plus SIEM breadth.
scenarios.hint: Which portal natively correlates endpoint+identity+email+cloud-app signals?

scenarios.title: The ransomware host
scenarios.situation: Ransomware is encrypting files on a workstation right now.
scenarios.prompt: What is the immediate containment action in Defender for Endpoint?
choices: Isolate the device — cuts network except to Defender, stopping lateral movement and C2
Delete the device object
Reimage immediately (destroys forensic evidence)
Email the user
scenarios.why: Device isolation is the first containment: it severs attacker connectivity while preserving the machine for forensics. Reimaging before evidence collection destroys the investigation; isolation buys time to scope.
scenarios.hint: What's the first click when ransomware is actively encrypting?

scenarios.title: The DCSync attempt
scenarios.situation: Defender for Identity flags a DCSync replication attempt from a non-domain-controller host.
scenarios.prompt: What does this indicate?
choices: Credential theft in progress — an attacker mimicking a DC to pull password hashes; isolate the host and rotate KRBTGT
Normal replication
A misconfigured printer
A backup running
scenarios.why: DCSync from a non-DC is a classic credential-dumping technique (Mimikatz-style) — one of the highest-fidelity identity alerts. Response: isolate, hunt for lateral movement, and consider KRBTGT reset (twice) to invalidate golden tickets.
scenarios.hint: Non-DC doing DC replication — what attack is this?

scenarios.title: The malicious link
scenarios.situation: A user clicked a link; Defender for Office 365 detonated it as malicious after delivery (ZAP).
scenarios.prompt: What already happened automatically, and what's next?
choices: Zero-hour auto purge removed the mail post-delivery; next: check who else got/clicked it and hunt the campaign
Nothing — the user is safe
Delete the user's mailbox
Disable email for everyone
scenarios.why: Defender for Office 365's ZAP retroactively purges malicious mail after detonation verdicts. The analyst's job: scope the campaign (other recipients, clicks), not just the one mailbox — attacks are rarely single-target.
scenarios.hint: Post-delivery purge fired. What scoping comes next?

scenarios.title: The shadow IT
scenarios.situation: Employees use an unsanctioned file-sharing app; IT has no visibility into uploads.
scenarios.prompt: What discovers and governs it?
choices: Defender for Cloud Apps — app discovery via logs/proxy, risk scoring, and session policies
Blocking all websites
Asking employees nicely
Ignoring it
scenarios.why: Defender for Cloud Apps (CASB) discovers shadow IT from firewall/proxy logs, scores app risk, and enforces session policies (block downloads, require MFA) on sanctioned/unsanctioned apps — visibility first, control second.
scenarios.hint: Which CASB discovers unsanctioned apps and governs sessions?

scenarios.title: The unpatched fleet
scenarios.situation: The SOC needs to know which devices are exposed to a newly announced critical CVE right now.
scenarios.prompt: Where do they look?
choices: Defender Vulnerability Management (threat & vulnerability management) — device exposure scored against active threats
A spreadsheet inventory
The news
Guessing
scenarios.why: TVM continuously assesses device vulnerabilities and correlates exposure with active threat intelligence — 'which of my devices does this CVE actually threaten?' Prioritization beats raw CVE counts.
scenarios.hint: Which capability maps CVEs to your actual exposed devices?

scenarios.title: The STIX feed
scenarios.situation: The team buys a premium threat feed in STIX/TAXII format and wants indicators auto-matched against logs.
scenarios.prompt: How does Sentinel consume it?
choices: Threat intelligence platform (TAXII/STIX connectors) — indicators land in ThreatIntelligenceIndicator and match in analytics/hunting
Manual copy-paste
Email alerts
A spreadsheet
scenarios.why: Sentinel's TI connectors ingest STIX/TAXII feeds into the threat intelligence tables; matching rules and the TI blade correlate indicators against your logs. Structured intel becomes detection, not reading material.
scenarios.hint: How do STIX indicators become queryable detections?

scenarios.title: The stale indicator
scenarios.situation: An indicator from 2019 fires on a partner's IP, causing a false-positive incident.
scenarios.prompt: What indicator hygiene prevents this?
choices: Indicator lifecycle management — confidence scores, expiry/revoked status, and source reliability weighting
Treating all indicators as eternal truth
More indicators
Deleting threat intel
scenarios.why: Indicators decay: IPs get reassigned, domains get cleaned. Mature TI practice expires/revokes stale indicators, weights by source confidence, and tunes matching rules — otherwise intel becomes a false-positive generator.
scenarios.hint: A 2019 IP indicator fires today. What lifecycle step was missed?

scenarios.title: The named group
scenarios.situation: Leadership asks: 'Are we exposed to APT29's current tooling?'
scenarios.prompt: What is the analyst's structured approach?
choices: Map the group's MITRE ATT&CK TTPs → hunt each technique in your telemetry → gap analysis on missing log sources
Google the group name
Buy a new tool
Say 'probably not'
scenarios.why: Threat-informed defense: translate actor intel into ATT&CK techniques, hunt each in your data, and the gaps you find (no logs for that technique) become the detection-engineering roadmap. That's the intel-to-defense pipeline.
scenarios.hint: How do you turn 'are we exposed to APT29' into an actionable hunt?

scenarios.title: The industry share
scenarios.situation: A peer bank shares IOCs from an attack; the SOC wants them in detections within the hour.
scenarios.prompt: What operational flow enables this?
choices: TI ingestion pipeline → automatic matching rules → analyst-validated incidents — with sharing agreements and TLP handling
Email forwarding
A phone call
Waiting for the vendor
scenarios.why: Operational intel sharing needs a pipeline (ingest → normalize → match → alert) plus process (TLP classification, source trust, analyst validation). Speed comes from the pipeline; safety from the validation step.
scenarios.hint: Peer shares IOCs. What turns them into detections in an hour?

scenarios.title: The intrusion analysis
scenarios.situation: An incident has attacker IPs, malware hashes, victim hosts, and a phishing lure — the analyst needs a model relating them.
scenarios.prompt: Which analytic model structures this?
choices: The Diamond Model — adversary, capability, infrastructure, victim with relationships
A timeline only
A list of IOCs
The kill chain alone
scenarios.why: The Diamond Model structures intrusions as relationships between adversary, capability, infrastructure, and victim — pivoting on any vertex (e.g., one infrastructure IP → other victims). IOC lists are flat; the diamond is relational.
scenarios.hint: Which model relates adversary, capability, infrastructure, and victim?

scenarios.title: The missed stage
scenarios.situation: A breach review shows the attacker was present for 200 days; early reconnaissance alerts were ignored.
scenarios.prompt: What framework would have organized the early warnings?
choices: The Cyber Kill Chain (or ATT&CK) — recognizing reconnaissance/delivery as stages of one campaign, not isolated noise
More firewalls
A bigger SIEM
Longer passwords
scenarios.why: Kill-chain thinking connects early-stage alerts (recon, weaponization, delivery) into campaign context — the 'boring' early alerts are the cheapest point to break the chain. Dwell time shrinks when early stages are treated as campaign signals.
scenarios.hint: How do you connect ignored recon alerts to the eventual breach?

scenarios.title: The worm suspicion
scenarios.situation: One server shows worm-like lateral movement attempts to 50 hosts.
scenarios.prompt: What is the containment priority order?
choices: Isolate the source host first (stop the spread), then hunt the 50 targets for successful compromise — don't reimage the source before memory forensics
Reimage all 51 machines immediately
Disconnect the whole datacenter
Wait and watch
scenarios.why: Contain the spreader first, preserve evidence (memory capture before reimage), then determine which targets were actually breached. Mass reimaging destroys forensics and may miss persistence elsewhere.
scenarios.hint: Source isolated — what evidence do you preserve before rebuilding it?

scenarios.title: The legal hold
scenarios.situation: HR and legal say the compromised executive laptop is evidence in a potential lawsuit.
scenarios.prompt: What must the responder ensure?
choices: Chain of custody — documented handling, forensic images (not the original) for analysis, legal hold on logs
Analyzing the original laptop directly
Letting IT reimage it
Emailing the disk image around
scenarios.why: Legal-bound evidence needs chain of custody: write-blocked forensic images, hashed and documented at every handoff, with log retention under legal hold. Analyzing the original or casual handling can render evidence inadmissible.
scenarios.hint: What makes digital evidence admissible?

scenarios.title: The persistent backdoor
scenarios.situation: A compromised server is cleaned of malware but gets reinfected within hours.
scenarios.prompt: What was missed?
choices: Persistence mechanisms — scheduled tasks, services, WMI subscriptions, registry run keys; eradication means finding ALL footholds, not just the payload
The antivirus is broken
The server is haunted
More RAM
scenarios.why: Reinfection means persistence survived: attackers plant multiple footholds (scheduled tasks, services, WMI event subscriptions, startup keys). Eradication is a hunt for every persistence mechanism, verified by monitoring for recurrence.
scenarios.hint: Cleaned but reinfected — what did eradication miss?

scenarios.title: The rushed restore
scenarios.situation: IT wants compromised systems back online immediately after malware removal.
scenarios.prompt: What must happen before restoration?
choices: Verify eradication (no persistence, clean images or rebuilt from known-good), reset credentials, and monitor — recovery without verification invites round two
Restore from last night's backup (which may contain the backdoor)
Change one password
Go live and hope
scenarios.why: Recovery requires verified-clean state: rebuild from known-good media or verified-clean backups (backups may predate or contain the intrusion), rotate all potentially exposed credentials, and heighten monitoring. Speed without verification is re-compromise.
scenarios.hint: Why might 'last night's backup' be unsafe to restore?

scenarios.title: The repeated phishing
scenarios.situation: The third phishing-driven incident this quarter used the same lure theme.
scenarios.prompt: What closes the loop?
choices: Lessons-learned / retrospective — root causes (why did controls fail three times?) become detection, training, and control improvements
A fourth incident report nobody reads
Blaming users
A new firewall
scenarios.why: Post-incident reviews convert incidents into systemic fixes: missed detections become analytics rules, control gaps become projects, patterns become threat intel. Without this, the SOC just relives the same incident quarterly.
scenarios.hint: Same lure, third time — what process turns incidents into improvement?

scenarios.title: The untested plan
scenarios.situation: The IR plan is a 40-page document nobody has ever exercised.
scenarios.prompt: What validates it before a real breach?
choices: Tabletop exercises — scenario walkthroughs with all stakeholders finding plan gaps safely
A real breach
Reading it once a year
A longer document
scenarios.why: Tabletops exercise the plan (roles, comms, decisions, legal/ PR involvement) without real consequences — surfacing the gaps a document review never finds, like 'who calls the insurer at 2 AM?'

lessons.title: Security Operations (SOC) — Core concepts
concepts: Sentinel is a cloud SIEM + SOAR: data connectors ingest telemetry, analytic rules generate alerts, incidents group related alerts into investigations, and automation (rules + Logic App playbooks) drives response.
Alerts are detections; incidents are the investigation unit. Correlating alerts by entity and time turns fragments — a risky sign-in, a malware hit, a mass download — into one attack story.

KQL is the hunting language: filter with where, aggregate with summarize, pivot attacks by reshaping dimensions. Password sprays reveal themselves grouped by source IP across many accounts, not by per-user failure counts.
Entities (accounts, hosts, IPs, URLs) are the join keys across products: follow the shared entity to stitch Defender, Entra ID, and Cloud Apps telemetry into a single timeline.
Defender XDR unifies endpoint, identity, email, and cloud-app signals with advanced hunting over one schema — join EmailEvents to DeviceProcessEvents to prove delivery-to-execution chains.
SOAR layering: automation rules do light incident triage at creation (assign, set severity); playbooks orchestrate multi-step response (isolate host, revoke sessions, ticket) across connectors.

lessons.title: How to Use This Microsoft Security Operations Analyst Bootcamp

What 'security operations analyst' means in practice: this bootcamp prepares you for the real-world responsibilities of a security operations analyst, not just exam questions. The SC-200 Microsoft Security Operations Analyst exam strategy: (a) first pass — read every lesson in order without skipping, taking notes on concepts that feel unfamiliar; (b) second pass — work every scenario and lab, reading the 'why' explanations even for correct answers; (c) final pass — take the timed mock under realistic conditions (no pauses, no references).

How to read the scenarios: every scenario has a 'why' explanation — read it even when you got the answer right, because it explains the WRONG answers too (and real exams design wrong answers from those same misconceptions). The hint is there to unblock you, not to give away the answer.

Active recall beats re-reading: after each lesson, close the page and explain the key concepts out loud in your own words. If you can't explain it simply, you don't understand it yet — re-read that section.

Week 2: Remaining domains (lessons + scenarios)
Week 3: All labs + weak-area review
Week 4: Timed mock → review misses → targeted re-study

lessons.title: Microsoft Security Operations Analyst: Field Overview and Key Terminology

Strong answer: 'X works by [mechanism]. In practice, I've used it to [application]. The key consideration is [tradeoff].'

lessons.title: Study Strategy: From Learning to Mastery
concepts: The learning pyramid: reading alone retains ~10%, but teaching someone else retains ~90%. After each domain, explain the concepts to an imaginary colleague — or better, a real one.
Deliberate practice: don't just re-read weak areas, actively test yourself on them. The scenario drills are designed for this — they force retrieval, not recognition.
Error analysis: every wrong answer is data. Log your misses by domain and concept. Patterns in your errors reveal exactly where to focus.
The 80/20 rule: 80% of exam/interview questions come from 20% of the material — the core concepts that everything else builds on. This bootcamp front-loads those in the early domains.

  0-10:  Review previous session's key concepts (retrieval)
  10-40: New lesson + scenario practice (learning)
  40-50: Lab exercise (application)
  50-60: Write summary notes (consolidation)

lessons.title: What Success Looks Like: Exam and Interview Readiness

The night before: no new material. Review your error log, skim key concept summaries, and rest. Confidence comes from preparation, not last-minute cramming.

lessons.title: Capstone Project: Build Your Microsoft Security Operations Analyst Portfolio Piece

lessons.title: Presenting Your Work: From Build to Interview Story
concepts: The STAR method for technical stories: Situation (context) → Task (your responsibility) → Action (what you did, specifically) → Result (measurable outcome).
Lead with the problem, not the technology. 'We needed to automate X because manual process took Y hours' is more compelling than 'I used tool Z.'
Quantify everything: time saved, errors reduced, performance improved, users served. Numbers make stories credible and memorable.

Weak: 'I built a thing with React.'

lessons.title: Joins and Lookups
concepts: join combines tables on a key — inner (default), leftouter, rightouter, anti (find missing)
lookup is simpler for enrichment — like a left join but optimized for dimension tables
let statements create variables and subqueries — essential for readable complex queries
materialize() caches subquery results — critical for performance on large datasets

example.walkthrough: materialize() runs the subquery once and caches it. Without it, the subquery runs for every row — catastrophic on large tables.

pitfalls: join without kind — defaults to inner; be explicit about what you want
No time bounds — always filter TimeGenerated first for performance
Subqueries without materialize — performance killer on large datasets
lessons.try_it: Write a KQL query that finds users with failed logins from IPs not in their usual locations. Use let and materialize.

lessons.title: Time Series Analysis
concepts: make-series creates time buckets — the foundation for trend analysis
series_decompose_anomalies finds outliers automatically — great for hunting
prev() compares to previous row — simple but effective for change detection
Time charts visualize patterns — the human eye catches what queries miss

example.code:
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| make-series failures=count() default=0 
    on TimeGenerated step 1h
| extend anomalies=series_decompose_anomalies(failures)
| mv-expand TimeGenerated, failures, anomalies
| where anomalies > 1.5
example.walkthrough: This finds hourly spikes in failed logins automatically. The anomalies column flags buckets that deviate significantly.

pitfalls: Wrong time granularity — 1h buckets miss minute-level attacks; 1m buckets are noisy
No baseline period — anomaly detection needs sufficient history
Ignoring seasonality — Monday morning spikes aren't anomalies
lessons.try_it: Create a time series analysis for a security metric. Identify anomalies and investigate the top 3.

lessons.title: Playbook Design
concepts: Playbooks automate response — Logic Apps with Sentinel connector
Trigger: Sentinel incident creation → Actions: enrich, notify, contain
Design for idempotency — playbooks may run multiple times; ensure safe re-execution
Test in a dev workspace — never deploy untested automation to production

example.code:
Phishing playbook:
  1. Trigger: Incident created (phishing classification)
  2. Enrich: Get email headers, URLs, attachments
  3. Check: URL reputation via Threat Intel
  4. If malicious:
     - Block URLs in Defender
     - Quarantine email from all mailboxes
     - Disable user if credentials phished
     - Create ticket for user education
  5. Notify: SOC channel with summary
example.walkthrough: Each step should log its actions. If the playbook fails midway, the next run should resume safely — not duplicate actions.

pitfalls: No error handling — API failures leave incidents half-remediated
Over-automation — auto-isolating hosts on every alert causes outages; keep humans in the loop for high-impact actions
No testing — untested playbooks fail during real incidents
lessons.try_it: Design a playbook for a common incident type. Include enrichment, decision logic, containment actions, and notifications.

lessons.title: Hunt Hypotheses
concepts: Start with a hypothesis, not data — 'I think attackers are using X technique in our environment'
Map hypothesis to MITRE ATT&CK — what technique? What data sources would show it?
Baseline normal first — you can't find abnormal without knowing normal
Document hunts — even negative results are valuable; they establish baselines

example.code:
Hypothesis: Attackers are using legitimate RMM tools for persistence
  ATT&CK: T1219 (Remote Access Tools)
  Data: Process creation logs, network connections
  Baseline: Which RMM tools are approved? Who uses them?
  Hunt: RMM processes from unusual users/hosts/times
  Outcome: Found 3 unauthorized AnyDesk installs → incidents created
example.walkthrough: The hypothesis focuses the hunt. Without it, you're just browsing logs hoping to get lucky.

pitfalls: Hunting without hypotheses — inefficient and hard to measure
No documentation — the next hunter repeats your work
Findings not converted to detections — the threat returns
lessons.try_it: Write three hunt hypotheses for your environment. For each: ATT&CK mapping, data sources, and success criteria.

lessons.title: Behavior Baselines
concepts: UEBA builds baselines per user/entity — login times, accessed resources, data volumes
Anomalies are deviations from baseline — not inherently malicious, but worth investigating
Risk scores aggregate anomalies — prioritize investigation by score, not individual alerts
Tune for your environment — generic baselines generate generic noise

example.code:
User anomaly example:
  Baseline: Alice logs in 9-5 from NYC, accesses HR systems
  Anomaly: Alice logs in 3 AM from Russia, downloads 10GB from finance DB
  Risk score: 85/100 (high)
  
  But check: Is Alice traveling? Did she get a new role? Context matters.
example.walkthrough: High risk scores need human judgment. The UEBA flags the anomaly; the analyst determines if it's malicious.

pitfalls: Treating anomalies as incidents — most anomalies have benign explanations
No baseline tuning — out-of-box UEBA needs environment-specific calibration
Ignoring low-and-slow — UEBA excels at detecting gradual changes that rules miss
lessons.try_it: Review UEBA high-risk users in your environment. For the top 3, determine if the anomalies are malicious or benign.

lessons.title: Cloud Security Posture
concepts: CSPM continuously assesses cloud configurations against best practices and compliance
Secure Score quantifies posture — track trends, not just absolute values
Misconfigurations are the #1 cloud risk — open storage, overly permissive IAM, unencrypted data
Remediate systematically: critical first, then high, automate where possible

example.code:
Common critical findings:
  - Storage account with public access enabled
  - SQL server without auditing
  - VM with RDP open to internet (0.0.0.0/0)
  - Key Vault without purge protection

pitfalls: Alert fatigue on low-severity — focus on critical/high with clear remediation

One-time remediation — configurations drift; continuous monitoring is essential

lessons.title: Multi-Cloud Security: Advanced Patterns and Architectures
concepts: Advanced implementations of Multi-Cloud Security follow established architectural patterns — learn to recognize which pattern fits which problem.
Composition over inheritance: build complex Multi-Cloud Security solutions by combining simple, well-understood components.
The tradeoff triangle: you can optimize for performance, simplicity, or flexibility — pick two. Document which you chose and why.
Refactoring Multi-Cloud Security code: the best time to improve structure is when you understand the domain better, not when you're firefighting.

example.code:
Multi-Cloud Security Architecture:
  ┌─────────────┐
  │   Interface │ ← What users interact with
  ├─────────────┤
  │    Logic    │ ← Core business rules
  ├─────────────┤
  │    Data     │ ← Persistence and state
  └─────────────┘
  Each layer has clear responsibilities and boundaries.
example.walkthrough: Separate concerns into layers. Each layer should be testable independently. When something breaks, the layer structure tells you where to look.

pitfalls: Mixing layers — business logic in the UI layer creates untestable spaghetti.
No clear boundaries — when everything talks to everything, changes cascade unpredictably.
Premature abstraction — don't build frameworks; solve the actual problem first.

lessons.title: Multi-Cloud Security: Performance Optimization and Scaling
concepts: Measure first, optimize second: profile Multi-Cloud Security operations to find actual bottlenecks, not assumed ones.
The most impactful optimizations are often algorithmic (better approach) not micro (faster code).
Caching is the highest-ROI optimization for read-heavy Multi-Cloud Security workloads — but invalidation is the hard part.
Scale horizontally when possible: stateless Multi-Cloud Security components scale linearly; stateful ones need careful design.

example.code:
Optimization workflow:
  1. Baseline: Measure current performance (p50, p95, p99)
  2. Profile: Identify the bottleneck (CPU? I/O? Network?)
  3. Hypothesize: What's the root cause?
  4. Optimize: Change one thing
  5. Measure: Did it improve? By how much?
  6. Repeat or revert
example.walkthrough: Follow this workflow for a real Multi-Cloud Security performance issue. Document the baseline, the change, and the measured improvement. If the change didn't help, revert it — don't accumulate complexity without benefit.

pitfalls: Optimizing without measuring — you can't improve what you don't measure.
Premature optimization — clean code first, fast code when profiling shows it's needed.
Ignoring the 99th percentile — averages hide the worst user experiences.
lessons.try_it: Profile a Multi-Cloud Security operation. Identify the bottleneck and implement one optimization. Measure the improvement.

lessons.title: Multi-Cloud Security: Security Considerations
concepts: Security is not a feature to add later — Multi-Cloud Security implementations must consider threats from the design phase.
Threat model: what are you protecting? From whom? What's the impact of compromise?
Defense in depth: no single control is sufficient. Layer authentication, authorization, encryption, and auditing.
The most common Multi-Cloud Security security failures are misconfigurations, not zero-days. Harden the defaults.

example.code:
Security checklist for Multi-Cloud Security:
  [ ] Authentication: Who can access this?
  [ ] Authorization: What can they do?
  [ ] Encryption: Is data protected in transit and at rest?
  [ ] Auditing: Can you detect and investigate misuse?
  [ ] Defaults: Are insecure defaults changed?
  [ ] Updates: Is there a patching process?
example.walkthrough: Walk through this checklist for your Multi-Cloud Security implementation. For each item, document the current state and any gaps. Prioritize by risk: what would hurt most if compromised?

pitfalls: Security as an afterthought — retrofitting security is 10x harder than building it in.
Default credentials — the most embarrassing and most common vulnerability.
No audit trail — when something goes wrong, you need logs to investigate.
lessons.try_it: Conduct a security review of a Multi-Cloud Security implementation using the checklist. Document findings and remediations.

concepts: Multi-Cloud Security rarely operates in isolation — integration with other systems is where real-world complexity lives.
API design for Multi-Cloud Security: version your interfaces, document contracts, handle failures gracefully.
Data format choices matter: JSON for readability, Protocol Buffers for performance, each has tradeoffs.

simulations.title: The impossible-travel alert
simulations.brief: Sentinel fires an impossible-travel alert: the candidate account signed in from two continents 20 minutes apart. Triage before you escalate.

steps.symptom: Impossible-travel alert on candidate@interstitium: logins 20 minutes apart, 4,000 miles apart.
options: Check for VPN or corporate egress that explains the geography before disabling the account
Immediately disable the account — impossible travel is always compromise
Delete the alert — these are always false positives
Reset the user's password and move on
steps.explain: Impossible travel is high-fidelity but not certain — corporate VPN egress routinely triggers it. Verify the egress story first; disabling the account on a false positive locks out a legitimate user.

steps.symptom: No VPN explains it; the second login came from an anonymizing proxy and then touched the storage account.
options: Disable the account, revoke sessions, and scope what the session touched
Just force a password reset — that ends it
Monitor silently for a week to gather more evidence
Email the user and ask if it was them
steps.explain: Confirmed compromise gets the full response: disable, revoke sessions (password reset alone does not kill existing tokens), and scope the blast radius via logs. Asking the user wastes the containment window.

simulations.debrief: You triaged like an analyst: verify before you act, then act completely — disable, revoke, and scope. Half-responses let attackers persist.

simulations.title: Ransomware in the SOC queue
simulations.brief: The queue escalates: ransomware behavior on a host with the artifact bucket mounted. You own the incident.

steps.text: Host is encrypting files and the bucket shows renames. First move?

choices.label: Isolate the host and block the bucket writes
choices.feedback: Correct — containment first, both the host and the data path.

choices.label: Start restoring the bucket from backup
choices.feedback: Restoring into an active encryption event just feeds it new files.

choices.label: Isolate host and block bucket writes
choices.feedback: Right — stop the bleeding before the transfusion.

steps.text: Contained. The ransom note demands payment in 48 hours. Call?

choices.label: Pay to recover faster
choices.feedback: Paying funds the ecosystem and often fails. You have versioned backups.

choices.label: Refuse, restore from versioned backups, preserve evidence
choices.feedback: Correct — versioning plus backups make payment unnecessary; evidence keeps options open.

simulations.debrief: You ran the ransomware response: contain, refuse, restore, preserve. That is the playbook that turns a catastrophe into an incident.

items: Eradication and recovery

simulations.title: The noisy analytics rule
simulations.brief: This Sentinel analytics rule pages the SOC 40 times a day. Review it and click the lines causing the noise.

steps.config:
Rule: impossible-travel-v1
1. Query: SigninLogs | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
2. Entity mapping: none
3. Threshold: 1 event
4. Suppression: disabled
5. Severity: High

issues.description: No entity mapping means alerts cannot be grouped or enriched — every event is a separate noisy alert.
issues.fix: Map the Account entity so related sign-ins correlate into one incident.

issues.description: Suppression disabled means the same user re-alerts every day with no deduplication.
issues.fix: Enable suppression (e.g. 24h per entity) so repeats consolidate.

simulations.debrief: You found the noise sources: unmapped entities and disabled suppression. Tune the rule and the SOC starts trusting the queue again.
